Monthly figures are rounded; these are scheduled entitlements, not individually verified deposits or exchange transfers. For each investor or contributor allocation, the published installments sum to the full grant: 6 × (3/48) + 30 × (1/48) = 1 That is six accelerated installments and thirty ordinary installments. Under the publicly described schedule beginning in October 2023, the last ordinary installment falls in September 2026. October 12, 2026, then marks the formal fourth anniversary. The distinction helps explain why some coverage calls September 12 the last investor and contributor release while Aptos calls October 12 the end of the cycle. On October 13, the official Aptos account stated that the schedule had concluded the previous day and that no genesis investor or core-contributor tokens remained to unlock. This is an attributable issuer assertion consistent with the original formula—not an independently reconstructed list of final beneficiary transactions. Where the 9.83 million APT disagreement comes from Once the investor and core-contributor schedules are complete, the unchanged original community and Foundation installments total about 4,543,478 APT monthly. That matches DefiLlama and Blockworks within ordinary rounding. Tokenomics.com’s 14,377,312 APT is about 3.16 times as large, a difference of roughly 9,833,834 APT. November 2026: published calendar estimatesTokenomics.com · Nov 1214.38M APTDefiLlama · Nov 114.54M APTBars begin at zero and compare forecasts, not observed token movements. Source: respective published calendars, reviewed November 8, 2026. The larger calendar’s recipient percentages offer a telling numerical fingerprint. Its reported 19.5% investor share implies roughly 2.80 million APT; its 27.5% insider share implies roughly 3.95 million. Those figures closely match the old investor installment of 2.808 million and core-contributor installment of 3.958 million. That correspondence supports a plausible interpretation: the model may be extending an expired schedule. It does not establish why the provider calculates the larger number. Its community component is also about 3.07 million APT above the original community installment. Tokenomics.com includes staking rewards in a broad community classification, raising the possibility that the forecast incorporates estimated emissions or another accounting category. A provider-level formula, dated source inputs and classification rules would be needed to prove the exact cause. There is a second denominator problem. Tokenomics.com’s page describes 2.1 billion APT as the overall scheduled supply through 2044. But the 2.1 billion figure is a hard supply cap, whereas the original one-billion genesis distribution and subsequent staking emissions are different mechanisms. Counting long-horizon potential issuance as locked scheduled vesting risks presenting a ceiling as if it were an already minted treasury inventory. Unlock, issuance, distribution and sale are not synonyms This is where unlock coverage often loses precision. A vesting event changes an entitlement or transfer restriction. Staking rewards create new token supply. A Foundation grant redistributes an existing balance. An exchange deposit transfers custody. An actual sale creates market flow. None of these events is interchangeable, and the same token can appear in multiple stages without representing multiple new units of supply. Aptos also changed its emissions economics in 2026. AIP-140 proposed reducing staking rewards and imposing a 2.1 billion APT cap. Later issuer updates describe a 2.6% reward rate and cap as implemented. These changes matter for forward supply modeling but do not themselves revive expired genesis investor grants. The most defensible reading of the 4.54 million figure is therefore deliberately narrow: it reconstructs the monthly community-and-Foundation schedule under the original terms, assuming those schedules remain applicable. It is not proof that 4.54 million newly sellable tokens will reach exchanges in November. The separate claim: 210 million APT permanently staked Alongside the unlock milestone, the Aptos Foundation announced that it would permanently stake 210 million APT and support its operations using the resulting staking rewards instead of selling the principal. In principle, that is a consequential change in the supply story. Permanently restricted principal should not be treated as ordinary future sale inventory. But the word permanently requires more than a pledge. Standard staking arrangements can include owner-authorized unlock and withdrawal functions, subject to protocol rules. Demonstrating that tokens are presently staked is not equivalent to demonstrating that the owner—or another authorized controller—cannot ever withdraw them. Blockworks’s October 20 research report described the 210 million APT as locked and counted it against undistributed Foundation and community holdings. That is an important published research claim, but the material available for this investigation did not establish a Foundation-authenticated mapping of the relevant staking accounts, deposit transactions, principal balances, and irrevocable withdrawal restrictions. A particularly revealing technical check concerns governance proposal #183. It has been cited in connection with the Foundation’s tokenomics reform. The published Move source for its supply-cap voting step identifies an empty governance proposal used for voting. Its execution does not, by itself, prove that 210 million tokens were transferred into a non-withdrawable arrangement. That is not evidence that the Foundation failed to carry out its commitment. A separate lock could exist. It does establish a limit on the common shortcut of citing the executed governance vote as sufficient proof of the permanent custody restriction. What would establish the lock?Authenticated Foundation-controlled account addresses; a complete balance reconciliation totaling 210 million APT; transaction hashes and ledger versions for the relevant deposits; deployed Move modules or resource-account authority records; and an explanation of whether any admin, owner, or upgrade path can release the principal. Staking reward balances should be identified separately. Why the remaining 210 million question changes the analysis Blockworks estimated approximately 335 million APT remained unvested in October, with 210 million supposedly permanently staked, leaving about 125 million for future distribution. Its implied remaining annual release pace was lower than the straightforward 54.52 million APT annualized from the original community-and-Foundation installments. Those figures should not be collapsed into one definitive schedule without reconciling which locked holdings overlap the original vesting buckets. If a permanent lock takes effect on balances already counted as future unlocks, a calendar can overstate sellable supply even if its mechanical vesting schedule is accurate. If, by contrast, the commitment covers previously circulating or separately classified stake, subtracting it from the remaining vesting schedule may double count the restriction. The distinction is economically meaningful. A permanently restricted token and a token freely withdrawable after a staking cooldown have different potential market behaviors. Yet neither behaves exactly like a burn while it remains in supply and continues earning staking rewards. The principal may be restricted while the yield is spendable—precisely the arrangement described by the Foundation’s operating model. What the calendars can—and cannot—say about price At a November 8 snapshot price of approximately $0.5952 per APT, the smaller estimate represents roughly $2.70 million of notional tokens; the larger one about $8.56 million. Those are illustrations based on the snapshot, not forward prices or forecasts of market impact. A calendar estimate is not a sell order. Even an accurately scheduled release does not reveal when holders will transfer, lend, collateralize or sell. A serious liquidity assessment would require the actual recipient accounts, transfer events, exchange inflows, bid and ask depth across venues, and evidence of subsequent execution. None of those can responsibly be inferred from a calendar countdown. The market may still price expectations before an event. That makes bad classification consequential: a trader reading a forecast of new investor supply may form a materially different risk expectation from one reading a community/Foundation-only installment, particularly when the headline total differs by almost ten million APT. What could overturn the preliminary interpretation? Tokenomics.com could identify a legitimate, distinct November tranche not covered by the original genesis schedule; publish a fully reconciled methodology showing why its current investor and insider labels remain appropriate; or demonstrate that the labels mean something broader than the original investor and contributor pools. Any of those findings would require revising the conclusion that its forecast appears to extend expired vesting entries. Similarly, Aptos could publish account addresses and immutable lock controls that decisively validate its 210 million commitment. An independently reproduced historical transfer and resource audit could settle the timing of the last genesis investor distribution. At the time of this report, neither the final beneficiary-level transfer trail nor the permanent-lock enforcement had been established from the identified public records. The Aptos Foundation has been sent a technical inquiry requesting custody addresses, transaction identifiers, withdrawal-authority information and an explanation of the November recipient categories. As of this research cutoff, no response is included in the record used for this article. A subsequent technical clarification would materially improve the supply accounting. My conclusion: accurate supply reporting starts with accurate categories What stands out to me is not merely the size of the conflicting numbers. It is how easily several true-sounding statements can become one misleading market narrative. Genesis vesting can be complete. Staking issuance can continue. A Foundation can promise to withhold principal. A tracker can still display a larger “unlock.” Each statement lives in a different accounting category. The original Aptos schedule, the issuer’s completion statement and the independent smaller calendars all point in the same direction: routine genesis investor and contributor unlocks should no longer be appearing as November 2026 releases. The larger calendar’s investor and insider amounts resemble installments from that completed schedule, but its exact calculation method has not been established. And the 210 million APT commitment remains a separate test of transparency. If the principal has been irreversibly locked, publishing the addresses and restrictions would let outside observers verify a meaningful reduction in available supply. Until then, the careful distinction is between a documented commitment and proven code-enforced permanence. For anyone using unlock dashboards to understand supply risk, that distinction is the story. blocks.text: One November calendar projects 14.38 million APT, including investor and insider allocations. Another projects 4.54 million. The original vesting arithmetic explains much of the gap—but the Foundation’s separate 210 million APT staking commitment poses a harder question.
Editorial illustration. The lock and calendar are symbolic, not images of a verified on-chain transaction.

Aptos says its original investor and contributor vesting cycle is finished. Yet a prominent public unlock calendar continues to assign November tokens to investors and insiders. The discrepancy is not a rounding error. It changes the apparent size and composition of the next supply event—and invites a larger question about how confidently the market should treat the numbers displayed on token-unlock dashboards.

The opposing estimates are striking. Tokenomics.com lists 14,377,312 APT for November 12, 2026, with 19.5% attributed to private investors and 27.5% to insiders. DefiLlama instead lists approximately 4.54 million APT for November 11, with community and foundation allocations. Blockworks independently displays 4.54 million APT for November 12 and marks the original investor and contributor categories fully unlocked.
Dates, release definitions and data-provider assumptions can differ. But the first test is simpler: do those purported investor tranches still exist under Aptos’s published genesis schedule?
Aptos publicly states that genesis investor and core-contributor vesting concluded October 12, 2026.
The original schedule yields approximately 4.543 million APT per month for continuing community and foundation releases.
The extra investor and insider portions in Tokenomics.com’s November projection closely resemble the old monthly vesting installments.

A separate Foundation commitment to permanently stake 210 million APT is documented, but a publicly reproducible account-level proof of permanent restrictions was not established in the available evidence.

Aptos published its tokenomics overview at mainnet launch in October 2022. Of the one billion APT minted at genesis, 510.217 million were assigned to the community, 165 million to the Foundation, 190 million to core contributors and approximately 134.783 million to investors.

The first two groups followed extended ten-year distribution schedules. The latter two had a twelve-month lock, six accelerated monthly installments, and then smaller monthly installments until their allocations were exhausted. The contract described a four-year lockup horizon; the arithmetic establishes why the final installment need not occur on the fourth anniversary itself.
Derived from Aptos’s original 2022 allocations and vesting terms. Monthly figures are rounded; these are scheduled entitlements, not individually verified deposits or exchange transfers.
For each investor or contributor allocation, the published installments sum to the full grant:

That is six accelerated installments and thirty ordinary installments. Under the publicly described schedule beginning in October 2023, the last ordinary installment falls in September 2026. October 12, 2026, then marks the formal fourth anniversary. The distinction helps explain why some coverage calls September 12 the last investor and contributor release while Aptos calls October 12 the end of the cycle.

On October 13, the official Aptos account stated that the schedule had concluded the previous day and that no genesis investor or core-contributor tokens remained to unlock. This is an attributable issuer assertion consistent with the original formula—not an independently reconstructed list of final beneficiary transactions.

Once the investor and core-contributor schedules are complete, the unchanged original community and Foundation installments total about 4,543,478 APT monthly. That matches DefiLlama and Blockworks within ordinary rounding. Tokenomics.com’s 14,377,312 APT is about 3.16 times as large, a difference of roughly 9,833,834 APT.

The larger calendar’s recipient percentages offer a telling numerical fingerprint. Its reported 19.5% investor share implies roughly 2.80 million APT; its 27.5% insider share implies roughly 3.95 million. Those figures closely match the old investor installment of 2.808 million and core-contributor installment of 3.958 million.

That correspondence supports a plausible interpretation: the model may be extending an expired schedule. It does not establish why the provider calculates the larger number. Its community component is also about 3.07 million APT above the original community installment. Tokenomics.com includes staking rewards in a broad community classification, raising the possibility that the forecast incorporates estimated emissions or another accounting category. A provider-level formula, dated source inputs and classification rules would be needed to prove the exact cause.

There is a second denominator problem. Tokenomics.com’s page describes 2.1 billion APT as the overall scheduled supply through 2044. But the 2.1 billion figure is a hard supply cap, whereas the original one-billion genesis distribution and subsequent staking emissions are different mechanisms. Counting long-horizon potential issuance as locked scheduled vesting risks presenting a ceiling as if it were an already minted treasury inventory.

This is where unlock coverage often loses precision. A vesting event changes an entitlement or transfer restriction. Staking rewards create new token supply. A Foundation grant redistributes an existing balance. An exchange deposit transfers custody. An actual sale creates market flow. None of these events is interchangeable, and the same token can appear in multiple stages without representing multiple new units of supply.

Aptos also changed its emissions economics in 2026. AIP-140 proposed reducing staking rewards and imposing a 2.1 billion APT cap. Later issuer updates describe a 2.6% reward rate and cap as implemented. These changes matter for forward supply modeling but do not themselves revive expired genesis investor grants.

The most defensible reading of the 4.54 million figure is therefore deliberately narrow: it reconstructs the monthly community-and-Foundation schedule under the original terms, assuming those schedules remain applicable. It is not proof that 4.54 million newly sellable tokens will reach exchanges in November.

Alongside the unlock milestone, the Aptos Foundation announced that it would permanently stake 210 million APT and support its operations using the resulting staking rewards instead of selling the principal. In principle, that is a consequential change in the supply story. Permanently restricted principal should not be treated as ordinary future sale inventory.

But the word permanently requires more than a pledge. Standard staking arrangements can include owner-authorized unlock and withdrawal functions, subject to protocol rules. Demonstrating that tokens are presently staked is not equivalent to demonstrating that the owner—or another authorized controller—cannot ever withdraw them.

Blockworks’s October 20 research report described the 210 million APT as locked and counted it against undistributed Foundation and community holdings. That is an important published research claim, but the material available for this investigation did not establish a Foundation-authenticated mapping of the relevant staking accounts, deposit transactions, principal balances, and irrevocable withdrawal restrictions.

A particularly revealing technical check concerns governance proposal #183. It has been cited in connection with the Foundation’s tokenomics reform. The published Move source for its supply-cap voting step identifies an empty governance proposal used for voting. Its execution does not, by itself, prove that 210 million tokens were transferred into a non-withdrawable arrangement.

That is not evidence that the Foundation failed to carry out its commitment. A separate lock could exist. It does establish a limit on the common shortcut of citing the executed governance vote as sufficient proof of the permanent custody restriction.

Blockworks estimated approximately 335 million APT remained unvested in October, with 210 million supposedly permanently staked, leaving about 125 million for future distribution. Its implied remaining annual release pace was lower than the straightforward 54.52 million APT annualized from the original community-and-Foundation installments.

Those figures should not be collapsed into one definitive schedule without reconciling which locked holdings overlap the original vesting buckets. If a permanent lock takes effect on balances already counted as future unlocks, a calendar can overstate sellable supply even if its mechanical vesting schedule is accurate. If, by contrast, the commitment covers previously circulating or separately classified stake, subtracting it from the remaining vesting schedule may double count the restriction.

The distinction is economically meaningful. A permanently restricted token and a token freely withdrawable after a staking cooldown have different potential market behaviors. Yet neither behaves exactly like a burn while it remains in supply and continues earning staking rewards. The principal may be restricted while the yield is spendable—precisely the arrangement described by the Foundation’s operating model.

At a November 8 snapshot price of approximately $0.5952 per APT, the smaller estimate represents roughly $2.70 million of notional tokens; the larger one about $8.56 million. Those are illustrations based on the snapshot, not forward prices or forecasts of market impact. A calendar estimate is not a sell order.

Even an accurately scheduled release does not reveal when holders will transfer, lend, collateralize or sell. A serious liquidity assessment would require the actual recipient accounts, transfer events, exchange inflows, bid and ask depth across venues, and evidence of subsequent execution. None of those can responsibly be inferred from a calendar countdown.

The market may still price expectations before an event. That makes bad classification consequential: a trader reading a forecast of new investor supply may form a materially different risk expectation from one reading a community/Foundation-only installment, particularly when the headline total differs by almost ten million APT.

Tokenomics.com could identify a legitimate, distinct November tranche not covered by the original genesis schedule; publish a fully reconciled methodology showing why its current investor and insider labels remain appropriate; or demonstrate that the labels mean something broader than the original investor and contributor pools. Any of those findings would require revising the conclusion that its forecast appears to extend expired vesting entries.

Similarly, Aptos could publish account addresses and immutable lock controls that decisively validate its 210 million commitment. An independently reproduced historical transfer and resource audit could settle the timing of the last genesis investor distribution. At the time of this report, neither the final beneficiary-level transfer trail nor the permanent-lock enforcement had been established from the identified public records.

The Aptos Foundation has been sent a technical inquiry requesting custody addresses, transaction identifiers, withdrawal-authority information and an explanation of the November recipient categories. As of this research cutoff, no response is included in the record used for this article. A subsequent technical clarification would materially improve the supply accounting.

What stands out to me is not merely the size of the conflicting numbers. It is how easily several true-sounding statements can become one misleading market narrative. Genesis vesting can be complete. Staking issuance can continue. A Foundation can promise to withhold principal. A tracker can still display a larger “unlock.” Each statement lives in a different accounting category.

The original Aptos schedule, the issuer’s completion statement and the independent smaller calendars all point in the same direction: routine genesis investor and contributor unlocks should no longer be appearing as November 2026 releases. The larger calendar’s investor and insider amounts resemble installments from that completed schedule, but its exact calculation method has not been established.

And the 210 million APT commitment remains a separate test of transparency. If the principal has been irreversibly locked, publishing the addresses and restrictions would let outside observers verify a meaningful reduction in available supply. Until then, the careful distinction is between a documented commitment and proven code-enforced permanence.
For anyone using unlock dashboards to understand supply risk, that distinction is the story.

bitcoin-monday-76000-pressure-test.text: Independent Market NotesBitcoin / Market structure8 November 2026 Market investigation · Pre-Monday briefingBitcoin at $76,000: The Monday Rebound That Still Needs ProofBitcoin stabilized near $76,000 after a sharp selloff, but ETF outflows, a misleadingly calm funding market and a rebound in open interest make one question unavoidable: is the selling finished, or merely paused?Analysis dated 8 November 2026Market observations through approximately 12:07 UTC8-minute read Bitcoin looked calmer on Sunday morning. That was the easy part to see. The harder part was deciding what the calm meant. After a rapid fall from above $80,000, the market was trading around $76,000, not far from lows that had already been tested. A quieter tape offered the outline of a bottom. It did not yet offer its proof. At approximately 12:06 UTC on November 8, the OKX BTC/USDT spot price was 75,990.30 USDT. In the preceding days, price had briefly fallen to approximately 74,888 USDT. The distance between those observations matters less to me than the terrain between them. Buyers were defending part of the decline, but the market remained below its short-term averages. The apparent stability was arriving just as a difficult week of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF redemptions ended. My working view heading into Monday, November 9, is therefore cautious, not categorically bearish. Bitcoin has demonstrated the ability to stop falling for a time; it has not yet demonstrated the capacity to reclaim the territory lost during the selloff. The distinction is the entire investigation. A selloff that changed the burden of proof The decline was not a simple, orderly retreat. In the OKX exchange-session series, the session beginning November 3 closed near 80,300 USDT; the following session closed near 76,039 USDT, a drop of roughly 5.3%. Subsequent sessions stayed close to $76,000. A market can build a base after such a move, but the preceding break creates overhead supply: participants who would have preferred to sell higher can use the next rally as an exit. That is why I care more about the quality of the next rebound than about its first few hundred dollars. The area around $77,000–$77,100 corresponds to a recent rebound high. Above it lies the seven-session average near $77,309. The twenty-session average was approximately $79,626. These are descriptions of historical structure, not walls where orders must be waiting. A fourteen-session average true range of approximately $2,324—about 3.1% of the observed price—also argues against overconfidence in a narrow Monday forecast. ATR measures recent trading ranges, not a guaranteed future move. A market capable of covering that distance in an ordinary exchange session can invalidate a neat-looking thesis quickly. A fragile recovery zone Price reference zones as of November 8Schematic vertical price map, not a continuous price chart. Historical resistance near 77,011; observed spot 75,990; local support near 75,395; deeper swing low 74,888 USDT. 77,011 — recent rebound high76,000 — nearby reference75,395 — recent local low74,888 — prior swing low Current point near 75,990USDT Levels are historical references and analytically chosen zones; this schematic does not depict order-book liquidity, liquidation concentrations or a realized forecast.Source: OKX BTC-USDT spot OHLC snapshots and completed exchange-session candles; session boundaries begin at 16:00 UTC. Wall Street demand was sending a less reassuring message Price alone can conceal the origin of demand. The week's ETF flows offered a different view. Reported U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF net flows for November 2–6 summed to approximately negative $1.282 billion. Four of the five sessions were negative. Friday, November 6, was reported at approximately negative $411.9 million. These were sizeable figures, and I would not dismiss them as a footnote. They suggest that the most visible regulated U.S. access channel was seeing net redemptions during a period when Bitcoin needed additional demand. But the flow numbers require care: trackers did not fully agree. A competing Friday tally of roughly negative $8.9 million apparently omitted the approximately $403 million IBIT outflow present in the larger estimate. The discrepancy changes the daily conclusion materially, so the larger number should be read as a reported tally rather than an independently reconciled final accounting. The reported ETF-flow sequence U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF reported daily net flows, November 2–6, 2026Reported net flow in millions of dollars: Monday minus 398.6, Tuesday minus 115.6, Wednesday plus 74.6, Thursday minus 430.2 and Friday minus 411.9. Friday figures are contested among trackers. $0 Mon 2Tue 3Wed 4Thu 5Fri 6*−398.6−115.6+74.6−430.2−411.9USD millions; reported daily net creations/redemptions *Friday's large reported outflow is disputed by a materially lower competing tracker. Chart reproduces the reported series used for this analysis rather than reconciling the conflicting feeds.Source: publicly reported U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF flow tracker tallies cited in the November 8 market dossier; attribution and reporting conventions differ. Accessible data alternative to the reported ETF-flow graphicSessionReported net flowNov 2−$398.6MNov 3−$115.6MNov 4+$74.6MNov 5−$430.2MNov 6*−$411.9M Nor is an ETF redemption automatically a same-minute Bitcoin sell order. Authorized-participant inventory, hedging and execution schedules complicate that transmission. What the figures can tell us is narrower and more useful: recent ETF demand was not an obvious source of support. What they cannot tell us is whether the next buyer at $75,000 will be a fund, a hedge, a market maker or somebody entirely different. The leverage market was not screaming panic There is a familiar shortcut in crypto commentary: rising open interest means bulls are piling in; falling open interest means bears are winning. Neither statement survives basic mechanics. Every open long has a matching short. Open interest counts outstanding contracts, not a net vote on price direction. On Hyperliquid, the BTC perpetual's hourly open-interest series fell from approximately 42,244 BTC at 00:00 UTC on November 7 to 41,563 BTC at 00:00 UTC on November 8, then rose to approximately 42,107 BTC by noon Sunday. That last twelve-hour increase—about 1.31%—is important, but it is not directional by itself. It shows gross exposure returning as price stabilized, not whether the returning risk is fundamentally long or short. The connected line is for readability; intermediate prices or OI states are not reconstructed.Source: Hyperliquid BTC perpetual hourly open-interest observations, November 7–8, 2026. Accessible data alternative to the open-interest graphicUTC observationOpen interest (BTC)Nov 7, 00:0042,244Nov 7, 06:0042,085Nov 7, 12:0041,824Nov 7, 18:0041,272Nov 8, 00:0041,563Nov 8, 06:0041,751Nov 8, 12:0042,107 The funding market was similarly subdued. On OKX, eleven of the twelve most recent BTC perpetual settlements were positive, yet the latest settled rate was only approximately 0.00336% per eight-hour settlement. Hyperliquid's sampled hourly rates were roughly 0.00125% per hour. The two contracts have different settlement clocks; comparing their raw percentages without adjusting the interval would mislead. Neither series, taken on its own, demonstrates dangerously one-sided positioning. The uncomfortable possibility is that leverage is returning before demand has convincingly returned. That is a risk hypothesis, not a verdict. A squeeze could follow if shorts are trapped; a fresh liquidation wave could follow if new longs are weakly margined. To distinguish those outcomes would require matched price, changes in contract counts, signed trading activity and liquidation evidence across a meaningful interval—not simply a funding print and an OI snapshot. What forty seconds of spot trading can—and cannot—say The most revealing small test was also the easiest to overinterpret. A window of 100 OKX BTC/USDT trades between 12:06:42 and 12:07:20 UTC on Sunday recorded approximately 0.3343 BTC marked buy-side and 0.4373 BTC marked sell-side. Based on the reported side labels, sellers exceeded buyers by 0.1030 BTC; buys accounted for 43.3% of the sampled volume. That is a real imbalance in the sample, not evidence that the entire market was under sustained selling pressure. The time window was less than 40 seconds, the volume was tiny relative to the broader BTC market, and the venue's trade-side labels were not independently reconciled against simultaneous quotes. The companion sample of 100 OKX BTC perpetual trades was closer to balanced: approximately 61.15 BTC buy-side and 64.45 BTC sell-side, a signed volume imbalance of roughly −2.6%. If the thesis is that heavy selling continues on Monday, those samples do not establish it. blocks.text: Bitcoin stabilized near $76,000 after a sharp selloff, but ETF outflows, a misleadingly calm funding market and a rebound in open interest make one question unavoidable: is the selling finished, or merely paused?

Bitcoin looked calmer on Sunday morning. That was the easy part to see. The harder part was deciding what the calm meant. After a rapid fall from above $80,000, the market was trading around $76,000, not far from lows that had already been tested. A quieter tape offered the outline of a bottom. It did not yet offer its proof.

At approximately 12:06 UTC on November 8, the OKX BTC/USDT spot price was 75,990.30 USDT. In the preceding days, price had briefly fallen to approximately 74,888 USDT. The distance between those observations matters less to me than the terrain between them. Buyers were defending part of the decline, but the market remained below its short-term averages. The apparent stability was arriving just as a difficult week of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF redemptions ended.

My working view heading into Monday, November 9, is therefore cautious, not categorically bearish. Bitcoin has demonstrated the ability to stop falling for a time; it has not yet demonstrated the capacity to reclaim the territory lost during the selloff. The distinction is the entire investigation.

The decline was not a simple, orderly retreat. In the OKX exchange-session series, the session beginning November 3 closed near 80,300 USDT; the following session closed near 76,039 USDT, a drop of roughly 5.3%. Subsequent sessions stayed close to $76,000. A market can build a base after such a move, but the preceding break creates overhead supply: participants who would have preferred to sell higher can use the next rally as an exit.

That is why I care more about the quality of the next rebound than about its first few hundred dollars. The area around $77,000–$77,100 corresponds to a recent rebound high. Above it lies the seven-session average near $77,309. The twenty-session average was approximately $79,626. These are descriptions of historical structure, not walls where orders must be waiting.

A fourteen-session average true range of approximately $2,324—about 3.1% of the observed price—also argues against overconfidence in a narrow Monday forecast. ATR measures recent trading ranges, not a guaranteed future move. A market capable of covering that distance in an ordinary exchange session can invalidate a neat-looking thesis quickly.

Price alone can conceal the origin of demand. The week's ETF flows offered a different view. Reported U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF net flows for November 2–6 summed to approximately negative $1.282 billion. Four of the five sessions were negative. Friday, November 6, was reported at approximately negative $411.9 million.

These were sizeable figures, and I would not dismiss them as a footnote. They suggest that the most visible regulated U.S. access channel was seeing net redemptions during a period when Bitcoin needed additional demand. But the flow numbers require care: trackers did not fully agree. A competing Friday tally of roughly negative $8.9 million apparently omitted the approximately $403 million IBIT outflow present in the larger estimate. The discrepancy changes the daily conclusion materially, so the larger number should be read as a reported tally rather than an independently reconciled final accounting.
Accessible data alternative to the reported ETF-flow graphic

Nor is an ETF redemption automatically a same-minute Bitcoin sell order. Authorized-participant inventory, hedging and execution schedules complicate that transmission. What the figures can tell us is narrower and more useful: recent ETF demand was not an obvious source of support. What they cannot tell us is whether the next buyer at $75,000 will be a fund, a hedge, a market maker or somebody entirely different.

There is a familiar shortcut in crypto commentary: rising open interest means bulls are piling in; falling open interest means bears are winning. Neither statement survives basic mechanics. Every open long has a matching short. Open interest counts outstanding contracts, not a net vote on price direction.

On Hyperliquid, the BTC perpetual's hourly open-interest series fell from approximately 42,244 BTC at 00:00 UTC on November 7 to 41,563 BTC at 00:00 UTC on November 8, then rose to approximately 42,107 BTC by noon Sunday. That last twelve-hour increase—about 1.31%—is important, but it is not directional by itself. It shows gross exposure returning as price stabilized, not whether the returning risk is fundamentally long or short.
Accessible data alternative to the open-interest graphic

The funding market was similarly subdued. On OKX, eleven of the twelve most recent BTC perpetual settlements were positive, yet the latest settled rate was only approximately 0.00336% per eight-hour settlement. Hyperliquid's sampled hourly rates were roughly 0.00125% per hour. The two contracts have different settlement clocks; comparing their raw percentages without adjusting the interval would mislead. Neither series, taken on its own, demonstrates dangerously one-sided positioning.
The uncomfortable possibility is that leverage is returning before demand has convincingly returned.

That is a risk hypothesis, not a verdict. A squeeze could follow if shorts are trapped; a fresh liquidation wave could follow if new longs are weakly margined. To distinguish those outcomes would require matched price, changes in contract counts, signed trading activity and liquidation evidence across a meaningful interval—not simply a funding print and an OI snapshot.

The most revealing small test was also the easiest to overinterpret. A window of 100 OKX BTC/USDT trades between 12:06:42 and 12:07:20 UTC on Sunday recorded approximately 0.3343 BTC marked buy-side and 0.4373 BTC marked sell-side. Based on the reported side labels, sellers exceeded buyers by 0.1030 BTC; buys accounted for 43.3% of the sampled volume.

That is a real imbalance in the sample, not evidence that the entire market was under sustained selling pressure. The time window was less than 40 seconds, the volume was tiny relative to the broader BTC market, and the venue's trade-side labels were not independently reconciled against simultaneous quotes. The companion sample of 100 OKX BTC perpetual trades was closer to balanced: approximately 61.15 BTC buy-side and 64.45 BTC sell-side, a signed volume imbalance of roughly −2.6%.

If the thesis is that heavy selling continues on Monday, those samples do not establish it. I would rather acknowledge the limit than convert a convenient burst of transactions into a predictive story.

The first is a price test. A sustained reclaim of $77,100 would challenge the immediate bearish reading, particularly if the market then holds above the roughly $77,309 seven-session average. A sustained break below $75,300, followed by a failure at the earlier low near $74,888, would make downside continuation more plausible. The operative word is sustained: a brief wick through a level has far less evidentiary value than repeated acceptance and corroborating activity.

The second is a participation test. Monday's U.S. session needs to show whether buying and selling actually expand around those levels; whether open interest rises because new exposure is opening rather than merely moving with the mark price; and whether the day's ETF activity reverses the preceding week's redemptions. A price bounce without better participation can still happen, but it earns less interpretive weight.
Select a hypothetical price condition. This is a research interpretation aid, not a live price display or predictive probability model.
Consolidation remains the defensible reading.
Watch whether spot participation and OI change reinforce one another. There is no confirmed directional edge inside this interval from the evidence presented here.

Macro timing adds another complication. Monday precedes the scheduled U.S. October CPI release on Tuesday, November 10, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. Treasury auctions and policy commentary can affect broader risk appetite, but I would not claim a single scheduled event has already dictated Bitcoin's next move. The more defensible point is that participants will be entering an important inflation release with price structure already damaged.

There is a credible bullish explanation for everything that looks weak. Large ETF redemptions may have been absorbed. The market recovered from a low under $75,000. Funding was not euphoric, so a reflexive crowded-long unwinding argument has less force. Open interest returning during stabilization could reflect hedges, short covering or outright risk-taking that ultimately supports a recovery. And an oversold market does not require a beautiful macro backdrop to stage a forceful relief rally.

The bearish countercase is equally straightforward. A temporary base below two short-term moving averages can become a pause before another leg down. Renewed leverage without durable spot demand increases sensitivity to bad news. If the market cannot reclaim its nearby rebound high while ETF demand remains negative, the path back toward the prior low becomes easier to imagine. Neither interpretation earns an automatic victory merely because it fits the last price move.

I am deliberately not assigning numerical odds to those paths. Doing so without a calibrated forecast model, a comparable historical sample and tested error rates would give the appearance of precision without its substance.

Bitcoin's next move will be narrated afterward as though it were obvious. For now the interesting fact is the mismatch between what the market makes visible and what it conceals. We can observe price, selected open-interest histories and reported ETF flows. We cannot infer the identities, conviction or constraints of the marginal participants from those measurements alone. We also cannot assume one perpetual venue represents the global derivatives market.

That is why I regard $76,000 less as an answer than as a stress point for competing explanations. If buyers reclaim the lost range with sustained participation, the market will have supplied evidence for a bottoming process. If the nearby lows fail while risk is being rebuilt, it will have supplied evidence that the calm was merely an interval between selling waves.
The lesson is not to forecast nothing. It is to demand that a directional thesis survive contact with the next observation. Bitcoin has stabilized. Whether it has recovered remains an open question.

mercado-bitcoin-hack-containment-timelin.text: Independent Market NotesInvestigations / Cryptocurrency custodyMercado Bitcoin Said the Hack Was Contained. The Wallets Kept Draining.The exchange announced rapid containment. Researchers say customer deposit addresses continued transferring funds. The unanswered question is who still controlled the signatures.November 7, 2026 · Independent Market Notes · Investigative analysisEditorial illustration. The sequence represents reported activity in the cited investigations, not a screenshot of a live transaction dashboard. On November 2, Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin said it had quickly contained a security incident. Blockchain researchers later traced transfers from thousands of customer deposit addresses beyond that public announcement. The real question is not simply whether assets kept moving. It is what the exchange actually stopped—and which signing capabilities an attacker could still use. There is a deceptively simple way to describe the Mercado Bitcoin hack: tens of millions of dollars moved out of exchange-associated wallets, investigators responded, and some assets were frozen. But that version misses the most troubling part of the record. According to Bitquery's November 5 reconstruction, Ethereum deposit-address sweeps continued until 16:56 UTC on November 2. Mercado Bitcoin's initial containment announcement was published at approximately 12:56 UTC. Nearly four hours separates those two reported events. In a custody system, four hours is meaningful only when we know what controls existed, which of them remained effective, and whether the attacker had already obtained independent authority to authorize transfers. None of those internal facts can be read directly from a public ledger. The later address sweep was much smaller than the headline theft. Bitquery attributed approximately $266,000 to 36,042 Ethereum deposit addresses. That disparity is part of the story: modest aggregate value can still expose a serious question about how transaction authority was distributed across thousands of addresses. The breach began as a hot-wallet incident Mercado Bitcoin, a major Brazilian custodial cryptocurrency exchange, confirmed an incident on November 2 and temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals. Contemporary Decrypt reporting described initial alerts from security firm Hypernative concerning more than $40 million in suspicious transfers across at least ten blockchains. Those figures were preliminary monitoring estimates, not final audited losses. In its November 2 operational update, the exchange described the affected environment as online hot wallets, not cold reserves, and committed to protecting customer balances. That is a significant assurance, but it answers an accounting and customer-remediation question. It does not, by itself, establish that stolen assets were recovered or that all compromised signing capabilities were neutralized. A hot wallet is designed to make operational transfers possible. Its accessibility makes it useful for withdrawals and consolidation, but it also means security depends on the implementation of signing, authorization, credential protection, and monitoring. A successful unauthorized transaction proves the asset moved; it does not prove whether a private key was extracted, an internal signing system was abused, or a privileged workflow was compromised. A timeline with two very different kinds of time The central chronology combines blockchain-research estimates with corporate and responder statements. Those sources document different things: a confirmed blockchain inclusion time, the time an incident-response team was contacted, and the time a public announcement appeared should not be treated as interchangeable events. Incident chronology. All times UTC on November 2, 2026 unless noted.TimeReported eventSource and qualification 06:24–06:48Ethereum hot-wallet funds moved outBitquery reconstruction; wallet attribution not independently replayed here 07:30Mercado Bitcoin representative contacted ChainalysisChainalysis account; firsthand report of contact About 08:00Law-enforcement outreach concerning freezable addressesChainalysis describes action within 30 minutes 12:27Ethereum deposit-address sweep reportedly beginsBitquery reconstruction 12:56Exchange publicly announces rapid containmentMercado Bitcoin announcement and contemporaneous coverage 16:56Deposit-address activity reportedly endsBitquery reconstruction; not an independent transaction-by-transaction audit The 12:56 announcement is not necessarily the instant internal containment controls became active. Likewise, a block timestamp is not necessarily the instant a transaction was signed or first transmitted. However, Bitquery describes a sustained sweep involving separate deposit addresses, not merely the delayed confirmation of one previously initiated payment. That distinction is crucial. The public data creates a specific question about continuing authority after the announcement. It does not tell us which internal responders knew about this particular exposure at what time. Why thousands of deposit addresses matter Exchanges often assign blockchain deposit addresses to customers but retain the credentials required to move the underlying assets. The addresses may be individually identifiable on-chain while the ability to sign outgoing transfers is administered centrally or through a delegated custody system. Users can see the address and account credit without possessing the address's private key. Bitquery estimates that 36,042 Ethereum deposit addresses transferred about $266,000 in total. Its analysis says about 91% of those addresses contained less than $10. Address count should not be translated into a count of distinct customers; one account can be associated with multiple deposit addresses, and the publicly reviewed evidence does not establish unique affected account counts. The meaningful point is technical. An exchange can suspend the customer withdrawal interface while an attacker with independent signing power can still move on-chain assets. A disabled website button is not the same as a revoked cryptographic capability. If usable private keys were exported, disabling the application that formerly stored or accessed them would not make those keys invalid. It is also possible that a compromised service continued generating signatures, or that an attacker abused a legitimate privileged transaction-management route. The ledger establishes the outgoing transfers as attributed by the researchers; it cannot select among these underlying mechanisms. What did “contained” actually mean? Mercado Bitcoin's initial public statement said it had identified and rapidly contained an incident in one of its systems. It also reported that customer funds would be protected and that deposits and withdrawals were temporarily suspended. There are several operational meanings of containment. Isolating a compromised machine can halt further access to that machine. Revoking administrative sessions can prevent continued use of those accounts. Disabling a signing service can prevent further signatures through that service. Moving remaining assets to new addresses can reduce exposure when existing keys are no longer trustworthy. These interventions address different failure modes. Taking the exchange offline can contain a business workflow. It cannot, by itself, revoke a copied private key. For ordinary Ethereum externally owned accounts, the original private key cannot be invalidated through an exchange dashboard. The defender would generally need to secure remaining assets through new authorized transfers, potentially while competing against an adversary for transaction ordering. Doing so across many small addresses may involve difficult operational coordination and transaction fees. Bitquery's attributed transfers challenge an expansive interpretation of “contained” as “all unauthorized movement had ceased.” They do not conclusively disprove a narrower statement that Mercado Bitcoin had isolated a system it initially identified as compromised. The unresolved question is whether public language conveyed the boundaries of what had actually been secured. The blockchain can show movement, not the signing architecture On-chain records can establish source and destination addresses, token transfer events, network fees, block inclusion, and successful state changes. They cannot show who had physical custody of a key, whether a hardware security module was abused, or which internal approval rules were bypassed. There is, however, one noteworthy point of convergence: Mercado Bitcoin's published address disclosure lists the EVM address 0xe485e7a70b1131216cb47ca4555c4bbb2c742478, also identified by Bitquery as a principal attacker destination. That corroborates a specific incident-associated address. It does not establish all the surrounding source-wallet attributions or the total amount stolen. At least three hypotheses fit the broad observations. The attacker may have acquired individual or derivable private keys. The attacker may have accessed a centralized service capable of signing without exporting keys. Or an attacker may have abused administrative permissions in a legitimate custody workflow. Distinguishing them would require signing logs, credential inventories, security-module records, authentication traces, and an internal reconstruction of policy changes during the incident. Bitquery also points to suspicious activity involving wallets it associates with BitMart. That is an investigative lead, not evidence sufficient to conclude that the incidents shared an operator, vendor, root cause, or attacker identity. The loss totals do not measure the same thing Early alerting, a company's balance-sheet accounting, and blockchain analytics can each produce different numbers without any one being automatically dishonest. The first may identify suspicious outflows; the second may use internal asset inventories and recovery classifications; the third may reconstruct transfers across known wallet clusters at historical token prices. Selected publicly reported figures; the scopes and valuation bases are not fully reconciled.SourceAmountWhat it purports to measure Hypernative, via early news reportingMore than $40 millionPreliminary suspicious transfers on at least ten networks Mercado Bitcoin, initial accountingAbout $38 million plus about $11 million blockedExchange-described unsettled and blocked amounts at that stage Mercado Bitcoin, later FAQAbout $36.3 million affectedExchange-reported affected asset value; methodology not fully specified Bitquery$48.6 millionAttributed historical-value outflows across 11 blockchains ChainalysisApproximately $49 millionIncident-response estimate associated with activity across 17 blockchains Bitquery describes the attacker-associated destination appearing across 17 networks, but attributes Mercado Bitcoin losses to 11. A wallet being active on a network is not equivalent to proof that Mercado Bitcoin lost funds there. Distinct address attribution policies can change both network counts and theft estimates. Similarly, asset values depend on the token prices used and the moments at which those prices are taken. Counting transferred units at transaction time is not necessarily the same as measuring the replacement cost later. A meaningful reconciliation would require a common inventory of transactions, wallet attribution, token prices, time windows, and frozen or recovered assets. For now, I would resist the easy temptation to select the largest published estimate and label it the definitive loss. The difference between these figures is itself a material unresolved finding. Freezing some tokens is not reversing the attack Chainalysis states that a Mercado Bitcoin director contacted the company at 07:30 UTC on November 2. It says investigators began tracing immediately and contacted law enforcement about potentially freezable addresses within 30 minutes. It subsequently described roughly $4 million in stablecoins restricted that morning, and about $9 million in freezes during the developing response. Bitquery subsequently estimated approximately $11.8 million frozen. Mercado Bitcoin's updates later described larger blocked totals. These are not necessarily interchangeable amounts: they come from different observation times and can reflect different definitions of “blocked.” Nor should they be added together as independent recoveries. Asset identification, transaction tracing, issuer restriction, legal seizure, return to a custodian, and replacement of a customer's account balance are separate outcomes. Stablecoin issuers may be able to blacklist specific token addresses through contract controls; they cannot apply those same privileges to native BTC or ETH. An exchange receiving tainted assets may restrict its own custodial account, but a finalized transfer on a public blockchain cannot simply be undone by a press release. These differences limit what the response totals prove. They show that meaningful interventions occurred in parts of the token ecosystem. They do not demonstrate full recovery or a universal capability to interrupt any asset flow. Could faster action have prevented additional transfers? The obvious criticism is that four hours passed between the announcement and the reported end of deposit-address transfers. But a clock alone does not prove preventability. A rigorous counterfactual needs the action that was available, who could perform it, when the relevant exposure was identified, and the last moment that action could affect a specific transfer. If the attacker relied on an active signing service, disabling that service before authorization might have stopped new signatures. If the attacker had already copied valid keys, shutting down the service might have done nothing to prevent direct signing elsewhere. If remaining funds could be moved to safe addresses, defenders might have competed to secure them, but their success would depend on control, transaction sequencing, fees, and operational readiness. Issuer intervention has its own narrow window: a supported token must still be within the issuer's effective restriction domain when a freeze becomes active. A token already converted or transferred out cannot be retroactively frozen at its previous address to prevent that completed movement. Receiving exchanges, investigators, and infrastructure operators can sometimes block downstream conversion or deposit routes. Those interventions may reduce the attacker's ability to monetize or move assets. They do not prove that the initial on-chain transfer was avoidable. My interpretation is that the reported timeline warrants a detailed internal explanation. It does not support a defensible claim that exactly $266,000—or any other specified amount—would have been saved by a particular earlier intervention. The prerequisites for that calculation have not been publicly established. The questions that would change the conclusion The unanswered questions are concrete. Were private keys extracted, or did an attacker keep access to a signing service? At what moment did the exchange learn that deposit addresses were exposed? Which signing pathways were disabled before the public statement, and which remained active afterward? What transaction-specific evidence establishes the earliest feasible rescue window? Which independently attributed transfers belong in the final loss ledger? And which announced freezes resulted in returned assets rather than merely immobilized tokens? Mercado Bitcoin also announced a phased website return planned for November 9, initially allowing balance viewing while other functions remained subject to validation. On this article's November 7 research date, that restoration was a stated future plan, not an observed completed reopening. The distinction between customer reimbursement and compromised signing authority matters beyond this one exchange. A company can protect account balances using its own capital while still needing to demonstrate that the technical path used to steal the original assets has been shut down. Containment is a claim about control What stands out to me is not simply that the chain appeared to contradict an announcement. It is how easily the industry compresses several different security outcomes into a single reassuring word. Mercado Bitcoin could have isolated a compromised environment while previously exposed signing capabilities remained usable elsewhere. That possibility is consistent with the records described by Bitquery, but it is not proof of a specific internal failure. The public chronology supports scrutiny; the public ledger alone cannot deliver a root-cause verdict. When a custodial exchange says an incident is contained, the decisive question is not whether ordinary customers can still press the withdrawal button. It is whether an attacker can still authorize the next transaction. The Mercado Bitcoin case demonstrates why those are not the same thing. What the evidence supports Bitquery reports Ethereum deposit-address sweeps continuing until 16:56 UTC on November 2, about four hours after the public containment announcement. Its estimate of about $266,000 across 36,042 addresses describes a separate phase from the main hot-wallet drain. Mercado Bitcoin, Bitquery, and Chainalysis report differing figures that have not been fully reconciled. The same identified EVM destination appears in the exchange's own disclosure and Bitquery's research. Some token assets were reportedly frozen, but freezing, seizing, recovering, and reimbursing funds are distinct outcomes. The public record does not establish a particular preventable transaction or the actual key-compromise mechanism. Research cutoff: November 7, 2026. Transaction-level chronology and multi-network amounts are attributed to the cited blockchain investigators unless expressly described otherwise. This article is an investigative analysis, not investment advice. Independent Market Notes · Evidence before certainty.

Those figures were preliminary monitoring estimates, not final audited losses.

In its November 2 operational update, the exchange described the affected environment as online hot wallets, not cold reserves, and committed to protecting customer balances. That is a significant assurance, but it answers an accounting and customer-remediation question. It does not, by itself, establish that stolen assets were recovered or that all compromised signing capabilities were neutralized.

A hot wallet is designed to make operational transfers possible. Its accessibility makes it useful for withdrawals and consolidation, but it also means security depends on the implementation of signing, authorization, credential protection, and monitoring. A successful unauthorized transaction proves the asset moved; it does not prove whether a private key was extracted, an internal signing system was abused, or a privileged workflow was compromised.

The central chronology combines blockchain-research estimates with corporate and responder statements. Those sources document different things: a confirmed blockchain inclusion time, the time an incident-response team was contacted, and the time a public announcement appeared should not be treated as interchangeable events.
Incident chronology. All times UTC on November 2, 2026 unless noted.

The 12:56 announcement is not necessarily the instant internal containment controls became active. Likewise, a block timestamp is not necessarily the instant a transaction was signed or first transmitted. However, Bitquery describes a sustained sweep involving separate deposit addresses, not merely the delayed confirmation of one previously initiated payment.

That distinction is crucial. The public data creates a specific question about continuing authority after the announcement. It does not tell us which internal responders knew about this particular exposure at what time.

Exchanges often assign blockchain deposit addresses to customers but retain the credentials required to move the underlying assets. The addresses may be individually identifiable on-chain while the ability to sign outgoing transfers is administered centrally or through a delegated custody system. Users can see the address and account credit without possessing the address's private key.

Bitquery estimates that 36,042 Ethereum deposit addresses transferred about $266,000 in total. Its analysis says about 91% of those addresses contained less than $10. Address count should not be translated into a count of distinct customers; one account can be associated with multiple deposit addresses, and the publicly reviewed evidence does not establish unique affected account counts.

The meaningful point is technical. An exchange can suspend the customer withdrawal interface while an attacker with independent signing power can still move on-chain assets. A disabled website button is not the same as a revoked cryptographic capability. If usable private keys were exported, disabling the application that formerly stored or accessed them would not make those keys invalid.

It is also possible that a compromised service continued generating signatures, or that an attacker abused a legitimate privileged transaction-management route. The ledger establishes the outgoing transfers as attributed by the researchers; it cannot select among these underlying mechanisms.

Mercado Bitcoin's initial public statement said it had identified and rapidly contained an incident in one of its systems. It also reported that customer funds would be protected and that deposits and withdrawals were temporarily suspended.

There are several operational meanings of containment. Isolating a compromised machine can halt further access to that machine. Revoking administrative sessions can prevent continued use of those accounts. Disabling a signing service can prevent further signatures through that service. Moving remaining assets to new addresses can reduce exposure when existing keys are no longer trustworthy. These interventions address different failure modes.
Taking the exchange offline can contain a business workflow. It cannot, by itself, revoke a copied private key.

For ordinary Ethereum externally owned accounts, the original private key cannot be invalidated through an exchange dashboard. The defender would generally need to secure remaining assets through new authorized transfers, potentially while competing against an adversary for transaction ordering. Doing so across many small addresses may involve difficult operational coordination and transaction fees.

Bitquery's attributed transfers challenge an expansive interpretation of “contained” as “all unauthorized movement had ceased.” They do not conclusively disprove a narrower statement that Mercado Bitcoin had isolated a system it initially identified as compromised. The unresolved question is whether public language conveyed the boundaries of what had actually been secured.

On-chain records can establish source and destination addresses, token transfer events, network fees, block inclusion, and successful state changes. They cannot show who had physical custody of a key, whether a hardware security module was abused, or which internal approval rules were bypassed.

There is, however, one noteworthy point of convergence: Mercado Bitcoin's published address disclosure lists the EVM address 0xe485e7a70b1131216cb47ca4555c4bbb2c742478, also identified by Bitquery as a principal attacker destination. That corroborates a specific incident-associated address. It does not establish all the surrounding source-wallet attributions or the total amount stolen.

At least three hypotheses fit the broad observations. The attacker may have acquired individual or derivable private keys. The attacker may have accessed a centralized service capable of signing without exporting keys. Or an attacker may have abused administrative permissions in a legitimate custody workflow. Distinguishing them would require signing logs, credential inventories, security-module records, authentication traces, and an internal reconstruction of policy changes during the incident.

Bitquery also points to suspicious activity involving wallets it associates with BitMart. That is an investigative lead, not evidence sufficient to conclude that the incidents shared an operator, vendor, root cause, or attacker identity.

Early alerting, a company's balance-sheet accounting, and blockchain analytics can each produce different numbers without any one being automatically dishonest. The first may identify suspicious outflows; the second may use internal asset inventories and recovery classifications; the third may reconstruct transfers across known wallet clusters at historical token prices.
Selected publicly reported figures; the scopes and valuation bases are not fully reconciled.

Bitquery describes the attacker-associated destination appearing across 17 networks, but attributes Mercado Bitcoin losses to 11. A wallet being active on a network is not equivalent to proof that Mercado Bitcoin lost funds there. Distinct address attribution policies can change both network counts and theft estimates.

Similarly, asset values depend on the token prices used and the moments at which those prices are taken. Counting transferred units at transaction time is not necessarily the same as measuring the replacement cost later. A meaningful reconciliation would require a common inventory of transactions, wallet attribution, token prices, time windows, and frozen or recovered assets.
For now, I would resist the easy temptation to select the largest published estimate and label it the definitive loss. The difference between these figures is itself a material unresolved finding.

Chainalysis states that a Mercado Bitcoin director contacted the company at 07:30 UTC on November 2. It says investigators began tracing immediately and contacted law enforcement about potentially freezable addresses within 30 minutes. It subsequently described roughly $4 million in stablecoins restricted that morning, and about $9 million in freezes during the developing response.

Bitquery subsequently estimated approximately $11.8 million frozen. Mercado Bitcoin's updates later described larger blocked totals. These are not necessarily interchangeable amounts: they come from different observation times and can reflect different definitions of “blocked.” Nor should they be added together as independent recoveries.

Asset identification, transaction tracing, issuer restriction, legal seizure, return to a custodian, and replacement of a customer's account balance are separate outcomes. Stablecoin issuers may be able to blacklist specific token addresses through contract controls; they cannot apply those same privileges to native BTC or ETH. An exchange receiving tainted assets may restrict its own custodial account, but a finalized transfer on a public blockchain cannot simply be undone by a press release.

These differences limit what the response totals prove. They show that meaningful interventions occurred in parts of the token ecosystem. They do not demonstrate full recovery or a universal capability to interrupt any asset flow.

The obvious criticism is that four hours passed between the announcement and the reported end of deposit-address transfers. But a clock alone does not prove preventability. A rigorous counterfactual needs the action that was available, who could perform it, when the relevant exposure was identified, and the last moment that action could affect a specific transfer.

If the attacker relied on an active signing service, disabling that service before authorization might have stopped new signatures. If the attacker had already copied valid keys, shutting down the service might have done nothing to prevent direct signing elsewhere. If remaining funds could be moved to safe addresses, defenders might have competed to secure them, but their success would depend on control, transaction sequencing, fees, and operational readiness.

Issuer intervention has its own narrow window: a supported token must still be within the issuer's effective restriction domain when a freeze becomes active. A token already converted or transferred out cannot be retroactively frozen at its previous address to prevent that completed movement.

Receiving exchanges, investigators, and infrastructure operators can sometimes block downstream conversion or deposit routes. Those interventions may reduce the attacker's ability to monetize or move assets. They do not prove that the initial on-chain transfer was avoidable.

My interpretation is that the reported timeline warrants a detailed internal explanation. It does not support a defensible claim that exactly $266,000—or any other specified amount—would have been saved by a particular earlier intervention. The prerequisites for that calculation have not been publicly established.

The unanswered questions are concrete. Were private keys extracted, or did an attacker keep access to a signing service? At what moment did the exchange learn that deposit addresses were exposed? Which signing pathways were disabled before the public statement, and which remained active afterward? What transaction-specific evidence establishes the earliest feasible rescue window? Which independently attributed transfers belong in the final loss ledger? And which announced freezes resulted in returned assets rather than merely immobilized tokens?

Mercado Bitcoin also announced a phased website return planned for November 9, initially allowing balance viewing while other functions remained subject to validation. On this article's November 7 research date, that restoration was a stated future plan, not an observed completed reopening.

The distinction between customer reimbursement and compromised signing authority matters beyond this one exchange. A company can protect account balances using its own capital while still needing to demonstrate that the technical path used to steal the original assets has been shut down.
What stands out to me is not simply that the chain appeared to contradict an announcement. It is how easily the industry compresses several different security outcomes into a single reassuring word.

Mercado Bitcoin could have isolated a compromised environment while previously exposed signing capabilities remained usable elsewhere. That possibility is consistent with the records described by Bitquery, but it is not proof of a specific internal failure. The public chronology supports scrutiny; the public ledger alone cannot deliver a root-cause verdict.

When a custodial exchange says an incident is contained, the decisive question is not whether ordinary customers can still press the withdrawal button. It is whether an attacker can still authorize the next transaction. The Mercado Bitcoin case demonstrates why those are not the same thing.
Bitquery reports Ethereum deposit-address sweeps continuing until 16:56 UTC on November 2, about four hours after the public containment announcement.
Its estimate of about $266,000 across 36,042 addresses describes a separate phase from the main hot-wallet drain.
Mercado Bitcoin, Bitquery, and Chainalysis report differing figures that have not been fully reconciled.
The same identified EVM destination appears in the exchange's own disclosure and Bitquery's research.
Some token assets were reportedly frozen, but freezing, seizing, recovering, and reimbursing funds are distinct outcomes.
The public record does not establish a particular preventable transaction or the actual key-compromise mechanism.

Research cutoff: November 7, 2026. Transaction-level chronology and multi-network amounts are attributed to the cited blockchain investigators unless expressly described otherwise. This article is an investigative analysis, not investment advice.
